reply.text: `==` tests whether two objects have equal values, by calling the `__eq__` method, while `is` tests whether two names refer to the exact same object in memory, comparing identity (effectively `id(a) == id(b)`). Two separate lists with the same contents are `==` but not `is`. `is` is the right tool for singletons like `None`, `True`, and `False` (write `x is None`, not `x == None`), since those are single shared objects and identity is what you mean. Using `is` to compare values such as numbers or strings is a bug: CPython caches some small integers and interned strings, so `is` may appear to work in testing and then fail on other inputs.
